basis.note: Read through a publisher's correlation table.

big_ideas.title: Evolution
big_ideas.text: Life changes over generations; shared ancestry explains the unity of life, and selection, drift and gene flow acting on variation explain its diversity.

big_ideas.title: Energetics
big_ideas.text: Living things capture, store and spend energy and exchange matter with their surroundings to grow, reproduce and hold a steady internal state.

big_ideas.title: Information storage and transmission
big_ideas.text: Heritable information in DNA (and RNA) is copied, passed on, expressed and regulated; cells and organisms also send and receive signals that change what they do.

big_ideas.title: Systems interactions
big_ideas.text: Parts interact at every level — molecules, cells, organisms, populations, ecosystems — and the behaviour of the whole emerges from, and constrains, those interactions.

practices.title: Concept explanation
practices.text: Explain a biological concept, process or model in words, both in general and applied to a concrete situation.

practices.title: Visual representations
practices.text: Read, explain and use diagrams, models, pedigrees, trees and other pictures of biological systems, and say what they leave out.

practices.title: Questions and methods
practices.text: Pose a testable question, pick variables and controls, and judge whether an experimental design can answer it.

practices.title: Representing and describing data
practices.text: Build and read graphs and tables, and describe the trends, patterns and relationships they show.

practices.title: Statistical tests and data analysis
practices.text: Do the calculation — ratios, rates, probabilities, frequencies, chi-square, standard error — and decide what the number supports.

practices.title: Argumentation
practices.text: Make a claim, back it with evidence and reasoning, and predict the effect of a change to a biological system.

topics.title: Structure of water and hydrogen bonding

los.do: Explain how water's polarity lets it hydrogen-bond to other water molecules and to polar or charged solutes.
ek: O pulls electrons from H, leaving δ− on O and δ+ on each H; each water can H-bond to up to four neighbours.

los.do: Connect cohesion, adhesion, high specific heat, ice floating and solvent power to hydrogen bonding and to a biological consequence.
ek: Cohesion + adhesion drive transpiration pull; high specific heat buffers temperature; open-lattice ice insulates water below.

los.do: Identify which elements each macromolecule class contains and where C, N, P and S enter biological molecules.
ek: C, H, O in all four classes; N in proteins and nucleic acids; P in nucleic acids and phospholipids; S in cysteine and methionine.

los.do: Predict which macromolecule class picks up a ³⁵S, ³²P or ¹⁵N label.
ek: ³⁵S marks protein only; ³²P marks nucleic acid (and phospholipid); ¹⁵N marks protein and nucleic acid.

los.do: Describe dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis as the reactions that build and break polymers.
ek: Joining monomers releases H₂O; hydrolysis adds H₂O to split them; enzymes catalyse both.

los.do: Count the water molecules released or consumed when n monomers are joined into, or cut out of, a linear polymer.
ek: A linear chain of n monomers has n − 1 linkages, so n − 1 waters.

los.do: Name the monomer and linking bond of carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids and triglycerides.
ek: Monosaccharide–glycosidic; amino acid–peptide; nucleotide–phosphodiester; glycerol + fatty acids–ester.

los.do: Classify an amino acid side chain as nonpolar, polar or charged and predict where it sits in a folded soluble protein.
ek: Nonpolar R groups bury in the core; polar and charged ones face water.

los.do: Distinguish saturated fats, unsaturated fats, phospholipids and steroids by structure and physical property.
ek: cis double bonds kink tails so fats stay liquid; phospholipids are amphipathic; steroids are four fused rings.

los.do: Tell structural from storage polysaccharides by linkage and branching.
ek: Cellulose β(1→4) straight chains H-bond into fibres; starch and glycogen α(1→4) with α(1→6) branches are compact and easy to hydrolyse.

los.do: Draw the structure of each of the 20 coded amino acids from its name, and name each from its structure.
ek: Every one is H2N–CH(R)–COOH; only R changes (proline's R closes back onto the N).

topics.title: Structure and function of biological macromolecules

los.do: Describe the four levels of protein structure and the interactions that hold each.
ek: 1°: peptide bonds; 2°: backbone H-bonds (α helix, β sheet); 3°: R-group interactions incl. disulfides; 4°: multiple subunits.

los.do: Predict how substituting one monomer changes a polymer's structure and function.
ek: Swapping a charged for a nonpolar residue (Glu→Val in hemoglobin) can change folding, binding and aggregation.

los.do: Identify the directionality of proteins (N→C) and nucleic acids (5′→3′) and why polymers grow at one end only.
ek: New nucleotides add to the 3′-OH; new amino acids add to the C-terminus.

los.do: Compare DNA and RNA by sugar, bases and strandedness.
ek: DNA: deoxyribose, T, double-stranded; RNA: ribose (2′-OH), U, usually single-stranded.

los.do: Write the complementary antiparallel strand of a DNA sequence and compute base percentages from Chargaff's rules.
ek: A pairs T (2 H-bonds), G pairs C (3); %A = %T, %G = %C, strands run 5′→3′ opposite ways.

los.do: Describe ribosome composition and explain why ribosomes in every cell point to common ancestry.
ek: Ribosomes are rRNA + protein, not membrane-bound, and make protein in all three domains.

los.do: Match the rough ER, smooth ER, Golgi, mitochondrion, lysosome, vacuole and chloroplast to their functions.
ek: RER: secreted/membrane proteins; SER: lipids, detox, Ca²⁺ storage; Golgi: modify and sort; lysosome: hydrolytic digestion.

los.do: Trace a secreted protein from ribosome through the endomembrane system to the cell surface.
ek: Signal peptide → RER lumen → transport vesicle → Golgi (cis→trans) → secretory vesicle → exocytosis.

los.do: Explain how an organelle's structure supports its function.
ek: Lysosomal pH ~5 suits its acid hydrolases; a central vacuole stores water and gives turgor; cristae add membrane area.

los.do: Relate the folded inner mitochondrial membrane and stacked thylakoids to capturing and storing energy.
ek: More membrane area holds more electron-transport chains and ATP synthases.

los.do: Calculate the surface-area-to-volume ratio of a cube, sphere or cylinder and compare cells of different sizes.
ek: Cube: SA/V = 6/s; sphere: 3/r — the ratio falls as size grows.

los.do: Explain why falling SA/V limits cell size and changes heat and material exchange in larger organisms.
ek: Volume (demand) grows as length³, surface (supply) as length².

los.do: Identify structures that raise surface area for exchange and explain the gain.
ek: Microvilli, root hairs, alveoli, intestinal villi and gill lamellae fold surface without adding much volume.

los.do: Explain how amphipathic phospholipids self-assemble into a bilayer and what embedded proteins add.
ek: Hydrophilic heads face water, hydrophobic tails face each other; proteins transport, receive signals, anchor and recognise.

los.do: Describe the fluid mosaic model and predict how temperature, unsaturation and cholesterol change fluidity.
ek: Unsaturated tails and higher temperature raise fluidity; cholesterol buffers it both ways.

los.do: Predict whether a molecule crosses a bare bilayer from its size, polarity and charge.
ek: Small nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂) pass freely; ions and large polar molecules need proteins; water crosses slowly without aquaporins.

los.do: Compare cell walls of plants, fungi and bacteria and explain how a wall prevents osmotic lysis.
ek: Plants: cellulose; fungi: chitin; bacteria: peptidoglycan; the wall resists turgor pressure.

los.do: Distinguish passive from active transport by energy use and gradient direction.
ek: Passive runs down the concentration gradient with no energy; active runs up it and needs ATP or a coupled gradient.

los.do: Distinguish phagocytosis, pinocytosis, receptor-mediated endocytosis and exocytosis.
ek: Bulk transport moves large molecules and particles in membrane vesicles and costs energy.

los.do: Explain how channel and carrier proteins move polar or charged substances down their gradients.
ek: Aquaporins pass water, gated ion channels pass specific ions; no energy is spent.

los.do: Tell simple from carrier-mediated diffusion on a rate-versus-concentration graph.
ek: Simple diffusion rises linearly; protein-mediated transport saturates when all carriers are busy.

los.do: Predict net water movement and the fate of animal and plant cells in hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions.
ek: Water moves toward higher solute concentration; animal cells lyse or crenate, plant cells go turgid or plasmolyse.

los.do: Calculate solute potential ψs = −iCRT and water potential ψ = ψs + ψp, and predict which way water moves.
ek: R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K), T in kelvin; water flows from higher to lower ψ.

los.do: Explain how contractile vacuoles, turgor and kidneys keep an organism's water balance.
ek: Freshwater protists pump water out; plants rely on turgor; animals adjust solute excretion.

los.do: Explain how the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase builds ion gradients and a membrane potential.
ek: Each ATP moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, leaving the inside negative.

los.do: Explain cotransport as transport driven by an existing ion gradient.
ek: The Na⁺–glucose symporter lets Na⁺ flow down its gradient and carries glucose up its own.

los.do: Explain how membrane-bound compartments let incompatible reactions run in one cell.
ek: Compartments keep different pH, enzymes and concentrations apart (lysosome vs cytosol).

los.do: Explain how internal membranes raise the area available for membrane-bound reactions.
ek: ER, cristae and thylakoids pack large reactive surface into small volume.

los.do: Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells by nucleus, organelles, ribosomes and chromosome form.
ek: Prokaryotes: no nucleus or membrane organelles, 70S ribosomes, circular chromosome; eukaryotes: nucleus, organelles, 80S, linear chromosomes.

los.do: Weigh the evidence that mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from engulfed prokaryotes.
ek: Double membranes, own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and division by fission.

los.do: Explain how the shape and charge of an active site make an enzyme specific for its substrate.
ek: Substrate must fit the active site geometrically and chemically; induced fit tightens binding.

los.do: Explain on an energy diagram how an enzyme lowers activation energy without changing ΔG.
ek: Enzymes stabilise the transition state; reactant and product energies stay the same.

los.do: Calculate an initial reaction rate from the slope of a product-versus-time graph.
ek: Rate = Δ[product]/Δt over the early linear region, before substrate runs low.

los.do: Predict how temperature and pH changes alter enzyme shape and reaction rate.
ek: Rate rises with temperature to an optimum, then falls as the enzyme denatures; each enzyme has a pH optimum.

los.do: Distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition and predict the effect of adding more substrate.
ek: Competitive binds the active site and is outcompeted by substrate; noncompetitive binds elsewhere and is not.

los.do: Read saturation and inhibition from rate-versus-substrate-concentration curves.
ek: Curve plateaus at Vmax; a competitive inhibitor delays the plateau, a noncompetitive one lowers it.

los.do: Explain how coupling to ATP hydrolysis drives an endergonic reaction.
ek: Coupled ΔG is the sum; transferring a phosphate to the substrate makes the overall ΔG negative.

los.do: Explain why organisms need continuous energy input and what happens when it stops.
ek: Order is maintained only by spending energy; energy loss leads to disorder and death.

los.do: Write the overall photosynthesis equation and locate the light reactions and the Calvin cycle.
ek: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂; light reactions in thylakoid membranes, Calvin cycle in the stroma.

los.do: Trace electrons from water through PSII, the ETC and PSI to NADPH and explain how the proton gradient drives ATP synthase.
ek: Water is split to replace PSII electrons; H⁺ pumped into the lumen flows back through ATP synthase.

los.do: Explain how the Calvin cycle spends ATP and NADPH to fix CO₂ into G3P.
ek: Rubisco fixes CO₂ to RuBP; 3 CO₂ in → 1 G3P out, using 9 ATP and 6 NADPH.

los.do: Read absorption and action spectra and calculate pigment Rf values from a chromatogram.
ek: Rf = distance pigment moved / distance solvent moved; chlorophylls absorb blue and red, reflect green.

los.do: Outline glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation with location and products.
ek: Glycolysis (cytosol) → acetyl-CoA and Krebs (matrix) → ETC and ATP synthase (inner membrane).

los.do: Explain chemiosmosis in mitochondria and O₂'s role as the final electron acceptor.
ek: NADH and FADH₂ feed the ETC, which pumps H⁺ into the intermembrane space; ATP synthase uses the gradient; O₂ + e⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O.

los.do: Predict how an ETC inhibitor or an uncoupler changes O₂ use, the proton gradient and ATP output.
ek: Inhibitors stop flow and O₂ use; uncouplers let H⁺ leak, so O₂ use rises while ATP falls and heat rises.

los.do: Compare fermentation with aerobic respiration by NAD⁺ regeneration and ATP yield.
ek: Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis continues: 2 ATP per glucose vs about 30–32 aerobically.

los.do: Calculate a respiration rate from respirometer data.
ek: Rate = O₂ consumed ÷ time (÷ mass); correct for the control respirometer.

los.do: Explain how molecular variation lets organisms function in different environments.
ek: Several chlorophyll types widen usable light; membrane lipid saturation tracks temperature; fetal hemoglobin binds O₂ tighter.

los.do: Distinguish communication by direct contact from communication by secreted chemical signals.
ek: Gap junctions and plasmodesmata join cytoplasms; surface molecules allow cell–cell recognition (e.g. antigen presentation).

los.do: Classify a signal as autocrine, paracrine, synaptic or endocrine, and recognise quorum sensing.
ek: Local signals act on neighbours; hormones travel in the blood to distant targets; bacteria sense density by signal concentration.

los.do: Identify reception, transduction and response and the molecules that carry out each.
ek: Ligand binds receptor → relay proteins and second messengers → change in enzyme activity or gene expression.

los.do: Explain how ligand binding to a GPCR, receptor tyrosine kinase, ion channel or intracellular receptor starts a response.
ek: Binding changes receptor shape; hydrophobic ligands cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors.

los.do: Explain how second messengers and phosphorylation cascades amplify a signal.
ek: One receptor activates many G proteins → much cAMP → many kinases, each phosphorylating many targets.

los.do: Describe the kinds of cellular response a pathway can produce.
ek: Change in gene expression, enzyme activation (glycogen breakdown after epinephrine), division or apoptosis.

los.do: Predict how a mutation or drug that alters one pathway component changes the response.
ek: A stuck-on component (constitutive Ras, cholera toxin on Gs) signals without ligand; a broken one blocks it.

los.do: Classify a described regulatory loop as positive or negative feedback.
ek: Negative feedback opposes the change; positive feedback amplifies it.

los.do: Explain how negative feedback holds a set point, using blood glucose or body temperature.
ek: High glucose → insulin → uptake and storage; low glucose → glucagon → release.

los.do: Explain a positive-feedback example and what ends it.
ek: Oxytocin in labour, ethylene in ripening, platelet clotting — each stops when the triggering event finishes.

los.do: Describe G1, S, G2, M and G0 and track DNA content per cell through the cycle.
ek: S doubles DNA (2c → 4c); cytokinesis returns each daughter to 2c.

los.do: Order the stages of mitosis and describe chromosome behaviour in each.
ek: Prophase condense → metaphase align → anaphase sister chromatids separate → telophase nuclei re-form.

los.do: Estimate time spent in each phase from counts of cells in each phase.
ek: Fraction of cells in a phase × total cycle time ≈ time in that phase.

los.do: Explain how checkpoints and cyclin–CDK complexes control passage through the cycle.
ek: G1, G2 and M checkpoints check size, DNA damage and spindle attachment; cyclins rise and fall to activate CDKs.

los.do: Explain how failed checkpoint control leads to cancer or apoptosis.
ek: Oncogenes are stuck-on accelerators; loss of tumour suppressors like p53 removes the brakes.

los.do: Track chromosome and chromatid number through meiosis I and II from a diploid cell.
ek: Meiosis I separates homologues (2n → n); meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

los.do: Compare mitosis and meiosis by number of divisions, products, ploidy and pairing of homologues.
ek: Mitosis: 1 division, 2 identical diploid cells; meiosis: 2 divisions, 4 distinct haploid cells, synapsis in prophase I.

los.do: Explain how crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation generate variation, and count assortment combinations.
ek: Independent assortment alone gives 2ⁿ gamete combinations for n chromosome pairs (2²³ in humans).

los.do: Explain why conserved genetic processes across eukaryotes support common ancestry.
ek: DNA as hereditary material, the genetic code and meiosis are shared by all eukaryotes.

los.do: Predict genotype and phenotype ratios of a monohybrid cross with a Punnett square.
ek: Aa × Aa → 1:2:1 genotypes, 3:1 phenotypes; Aa × aa → 1:1.

los.do: Predict dihybrid and multi-gene outcomes with the product and sum rules.
ek: Independent events multiply; mutually exclusive outcomes add; AaBb × AaBb → 9:3:3:1.

los.do: Determine the inheritance pattern from a pedigree and compute a family member's genotype probability.
ek: Autosomal recessive can skip generations; dominant traits appear in every generation; unaffected sibs of affected are 2/3 carriers.

los.do: Use a chi-square test to decide whether cross data fit an expected Mendelian ratio.
ek: χ² = Σ(o − e)²/e; df = categories − 1; reject the null if χ² exceeds the critical value at p = 0.05.

los.do: Predict cross outcomes under incomplete dominance, codominance and multiple alleles.
ek: Incomplete: blended heterozygote (1:2:1 phenotypes); codominant: both expressed (AB blood); ABO has three alleles.

los.do: Predict offspring ratios for X-linked traits by sex.
ek: Males are hemizygous: one X allele decides the phenotype; carrier mother → half of sons affected.

los.do: Recognise linkage from offspring counts and convert recombination frequency to map distance.
ek: Recombinants ÷ total × 100 = map units; linked genes give excess parental types.

los.do: Explain maternal inheritance of organelle genes and the continuous variation of polygenic traits.
ek: Mitochondria and chloroplasts come via the egg; many additive genes give a bell-shaped trait distribution.

los.do: Explain how one genotype can give different phenotypes in different environments.
ek: Soil pH changes hydrangea colour; incubation temperature sets sex in some reptiles; diet controls PKU symptoms.

los.do: Explain how nondisjunction produces aneuploid gametes and name resulting human conditions.
ek: A meiosis I error makes all four gametes abnormal, a meiosis II error two; trisomy 21, XO (Turner), XXY (Klinefelter).

los.do: Read sex and chromosome-number abnormalities from a karyotype.
ek: Count 22 autosome pairs plus the sex chromosomes; an extra or missing chromosome shows as 47 or 45.

los.do: Compare how genomes are organised in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
ek: Prokaryotes: one circular chromosome plus plasmids; eukaryotes: several linear chromosomes wrapped on histones.

los.do: Explain which features suit DNA to carry heredity and the experiments that showed it does.
ek: Complementary pairing allows copying and repair; Griffith, Avery–MacLeod–McCarty and Hershey–Chase identified DNA as the genetic material.

los.do: Describe semiconservative replication and the roles of helicase, topoisomerase, primase, DNA polymerase and ligase.
ek: Each daughter helix keeps one parent strand; polymerase needs a primer and adds only to a 3′ end.

los.do: Explain leading- versus lagging-strand synthesis and Okazaki fragments.
ek: 5′→3′ synthesis on antiparallel templates forces one strand to be made in fragments joined by ligase.

los.do: Predict Meselson–Stahl density bands after n generations in ¹⁴N medium.
ek: Gen 1: all hybrid; gen n: 2/2ⁿ hybrid, rest light.

los.do: Transcribe a template strand into mRNA and tell the template strand from the coding strand.
ek: mRNA matches the coding strand (U for T) and is complementary, antiparallel to the template.

los.do: Describe the 5′ cap, poly-A tail and splicing, and how alternative splicing yields several proteins from one gene.
ek: Introns are removed and exons joined; different exon combinations make different proteins.

los.do: Translate an mRNA into an amino acid sequence with a codon table, finding the start and stop codons.
ek: Read 5′→3′ in triplets from AUG (Met) to UAA, UAG or UGA.

los.do: Describe initiation, elongation and termination with the ribosome's A, P and E sites.
ek: Charged tRNA enters A, peptide transfers to it, ribosome shifts so tRNA moves P → E; release factor ends it at a stop codon.

los.do: Explain how regulatory proteins, histone acetylation and DNA methylation turn eukaryotic genes up or down.
ek: Acetylation loosens chromatin (more transcription); promoter methylation silences; these epigenetic marks can be inherited.

los.do: Predict lac (inducible) and trp (repressible) operon expression under given conditions.
ek: Lactose inactivates the lac repressor; tryptophan activates the trp repressor; the operator lies between promoter and genes.

los.do: Explain how a combination of transcription factors at enhancers sets a gene's expression level.
ek: Activators and repressors bind regulatory sequences; the particular combination present decides transcription.

los.do: Explain how differential gene expression makes different cell types from one genome.
ek: Every cell has the same DNA; different transcription factors switch on different gene sets.

los.do: Classify a point mutation as silent, missense, nonsense or frameshift and predict its effect on the protein.
ek: Insertions or deletions not in multiples of three shift the reading frame downstream.

los.do: Explain how a change in genotype changes phenotype, using sickle-cell anaemia.
ek: One base change → Glu→Val → hemoglobin polymerises → sickled cells.

los.do: Explain how replication errors, horizontal gene transfer and viral recombination create variation selection can act on.
ek: Transformation, transduction and conjugation move genes between bacteria; RNA viruses mutate fast.

los.do: Read gel electrophoresis band patterns to compare fragment sizes and match samples.
ek: DNA is negative and runs toward +; smaller fragments travel farther.

los.do: Describe the PCR cycle and calculate copies after n cycles.
ek: Denature (~95 °C) → anneal primers → extend with Taq; copies = initial × 2ⁿ.

los.do: Describe bacterial transformation with a recombinant plasmid and how restriction enzymes and sequencing are used.
ek: Cut vector and insert with the same restriction enzyme, ligate, transform, select on antibiotic.

los.do: Identify the conditions natural selection needs from a scenario.
ek: Heritable variation, more offspring than survive, and differential survival and reproduction tied to that variation.

los.do: Explain how selection on phenotypes changes allele frequencies and define fitness.
ek: Fitness is reproductive success; selection acts on individuals, but populations evolve.

los.do: Classify selection as directional, stabilising or disruptive from before-and-after trait distributions.
ek: Directional shifts the mean; stabilising narrows it; disruptive favours both extremes.

los.do: Explain how human choice of breeders or human-imposed pressures change a population's diversity.
ek: Selective breeding and antibiotic or pesticide use select for chosen or resistant traits.

los.do: Explain convergent evolution as similar selection in similar environments.
ek: Unrelated lineages evolve analogous traits (wings in birds and bats, fins in sharks and dolphins).

los.do: Distinguish genetic drift, bottleneck, founder effect and gene flow.
ek: Drift is random change in allele frequency; bottleneck and founder effects are drift after a sharp drop or a small colony.

los.do: Explain why chance changes allele frequencies more in small populations.
ek: Sampling error is larger with fewer breeders; alleles can be lost or fixed regardless of fitness.

los.do: Explain how mutation and gene flow shift a population's genetic makeup over time.
ek: Mutation is the ultimate source of new alleles; migration makes populations more alike.

los.do: Calculate allele and genotype frequencies with p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
ek: q² is the recessive phenotype frequency; q = √q²; carriers = 2pq.

los.do: State the five conditions under which allele frequencies stay constant.
ek: No mutation, no migration, no selection, random mating, very large population.

los.do: Decide from frequency data whether a population is evolving and name the condition that is failing.
ek: Observed genotype counts far from p², 2pq, q² (by χ²) or changing across generations mean evolution.

los.do: Describe the kinds of data that support evolution.
ek: Fossils, comparative anatomy, molecular sequences, embryology and biogeography.

los.do: Distinguish homologous, analogous and vestigial structures and date fossils from radioisotope half-lives.
ek: Fraction remaining = (1/2)^(t / t½); homology reflects shared ancestry, analogy reflects convergence.

los.do: Identify molecular features shared by all living things as evidence of a common ancestor.
ek: DNA/RNA genetic material, a nearly universal genetic code, ribosomes and core metabolic pathways like glycolysis.

los.do: Identify features shared by all eukaryotes as evidence of their common ancestry.
ek: Membrane-bound organelles, linear chromosomes and genes with introns.

los.do: Explain current examples showing evolution is ongoing.
ek: Antibiotic and pesticide resistance, seasonal flu strains, changing fossil and genomic records.

los.do: Describe the morphological and molecular evidence used to infer relatedness, and prefer molecular data when they conflict.
ek: Fewer sequence differences = more recent common ancestor; molecular data avoid convergence errors.

los.do: Read a phylogenetic tree or cladogram for most recent common ancestors, sister taxa and shared derived traits.
ek: Nodes are ancestors; relatedness is read from nodes, not from tip order.

los.do: Build the most parsimonious cladogram from a table of shared derived characters.
ek: Group taxa by shared derived traits; prefer the tree with the fewest character changes; the outgroup roots it.

los.do: Apply the biological species concept and distinguish allopatric from sympatric speciation.
ek: Species = interbreeding populations producing fertile offspring; allopatric needs a geographic barrier, sympatric does not (polyploidy).

los.do: Contrast punctuated equilibrium with gradualism and relate rate to adaptive radiation.
ek: Long stasis with rapid bursts vs steady change; open niches speed diversification.

los.do: Classify a reproductive barrier in a scenario as prezygotic or postzygotic and name its type.
ek: Prezygotic: habitat, temporal, behavioural, mechanical, gametic; postzygotic: hybrid inviability, sterility, breakdown.

los.do: Describe factors that drive a population to extinction.
ek: Habitat loss, rapid environmental change, disease, competition, small population size.

los.do: Explain how the speed of environmental change, including human change, affects extinction risk.
ek: Change faster than populations can adapt raises extinction rates.

los.do: Explain diversity as speciation rate minus extinction rate and how mass extinctions open niches for adaptive radiation.
ek: After the end-Cretaceous extinction, mammals radiated into vacated niches.

los.do: Explain how a population's genetic diversity affects its ability to survive environmental pressure.
ek: Low diversity (Irish potato monoculture, cheetahs) means one disease or change can hit everyone.

los.do: Describe the evidence for hypotheses about how life began.
ek: Earth ~4.6 Byr, life by ~3.5 Byr; Miller–Urey made organics abiotically; RNA can store information and catalyse (RNA world).

los.do: Explain how organisms change behaviour or physiology in response to environmental cues.
ek: Taxis and kinesis, photoperiodism, hibernation and migration time activity to conditions.

los.do: Explain how signals between organisms change behaviour and how cooperation can raise fitness.
ek: Visual, auditory, chemical and tactile signals; kin selection explains altruism toward relatives.

los.do: Compare endotherms and ectotherms and relate metabolic rate per gram to body size.
ek: Smaller endotherms have higher mass-specific metabolic rates (larger SA/V).

los.do: Predict how a change in energy availability changes population size and ecosystem structure.
ek: Less energy at the base shrinks every level above it; surplus energy lets populations grow.

los.do: Calculate energy passed between trophic levels and distinguish gross from net primary productivity.
ek: About 10% transfers per level; NPP = GPP − respiration.

los.do: Trace carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and water through their biogeochemical cycles.
ek: N₂ fixation → nitrification → assimilation → ammonification → denitrification; phosphorus has no atmospheric phase.

los.do: Calculate per-capita birth and death rates and r from population counts.
ek: b = B/N, d = D/N, r = b − d.

los.do: Calculate growth with dN/dt = r_max N and recognise a J-shaped curve.
ek: Unlimited resources give exponential growth; growth rate scales with N.

los.do: Calculate logistic growth with dN/dt = r_max N (K − N)/K and locate K on a graph.
ek: Growth is fastest at N = K/2 and stops at K.

los.do: Classify a limiting factor as density-dependent or density-independent.
ek: Competition, disease and predation scale with density; fire, floods and freezes do not.

los.do: Calculate Simpson's diversity index and compare communities by richness and evenness.
ek: D = 1 − Σ(n/N)²; closer to 1 is more diverse.

los.do: Classify species interactions by their +, − or 0 effect on each partner.
ek: Mutualism +/+, commensalism +/0, predation and parasitism +/−, competition −/−.

los.do: Interpret predator–prey cycles, competitive exclusion and resource partitioning from data.
ek: Predator peaks lag prey peaks; two species cannot share one niche indefinitely.

los.do: Explain how resource availability drives community change, including primary and secondary succession.
ek: Primary starts on bare rock with pioneer species; secondary starts on existing soil.

los.do: Explain why ecosystems with higher diversity are more resilient.
ek: More species means redundancy: if one fails another fills the role.

los.do: Predict the effect of removing a keystone species, a producer or an essential abiotic factor.
ek: Keystone effects exceed abundance (sea otters → urchins → kelp); losing producers collapses the food web.

los.do: Explain how environmental change selects among variants already present in a population.
ek: Heterozygote advantage (sickle-cell trait and malaria) keeps a harmful allele common.

los.do: Explain how an invasive species spreads and disrupts a native community.
ek: Freed from its natural predators and competitors, it outcompetes natives.

los.do: Describe how human activity changes ecosystems: habitat loss, biomagnification, eutrophication and climate change.
ek: Fat-soluble toxins concentrate up food chains; excess nutrients → algal bloom → decomposition → O₂ depletion.

los.do: Explain how geological and meteorological events change ecosystems.
ek: Volcanic eruptions, El Niño and impacts reshape habitats and can trigger succession.

units.title: Anatomy and Physiology
units.weight_est: DAT Biology: Structure and Function of Systems

los.do: Explain how a neuron generates and propagates an action potential.
ek: Threshold opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (depolarise), then K⁺ channels (repolarise); myelin gives saltatory conduction.

los.do: Explain synaptic transmission and match nervous-system divisions and sensory receptors to their roles.
ek: Ca²⁺ entry triggers neurotransmitter release; sympathetic = fight-or-flight, parasympathetic = rest-and-digest; rods dim light, cones colour.

los.do: Distinguish peptide from steroid hormone action.
ek: Peptides bind surface receptors and use second messengers; steroids enter the cell and act as transcription factors.

los.do: Match major glands to their hormones and targets and predict hypothalamic–pituitary feedback.
ek: Hypothalamus → anterior pituitary tropic hormones → target gland; the target hormone inhibits both upstream.

los.do: Explain the sliding-filament cycle and its dependence on Ca²⁺ and ATP.
ek: Ca²⁺ binds troponin, tropomyosin uncovers actin; ATP binding releases myosin, hydrolysis re-cocks it.

los.do: Predict bone and blood-Ca²⁺ responses to PTH and calcitonin, and name the skin's layers and roles.
ek: Osteoclasts resorb, osteoblasts build; PTH raises blood Ca²⁺, calcitonin lowers it; epidermis protects, dermis holds vessels and glands.

los.do: Trace blood through the heart and body and relate vessel structure to pressure.
ek: RA → RV → lungs → LA → LV → aorta; arteries thick and high-pressure, veins valved, capillaries one cell thick.

los.do: Predict how CO₂, pH and temperature shift the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve.
ek: ↑CO₂, ↑H⁺, ↑temperature shift right (lower affinity, more unloading — Bohr effect).

los.do: Explain ventilation, alveolar gas exchange and how blood CO₂ sets breathing rate.
ek: Diaphragm contracts → chest volume up, pressure down → air in; medulla responds to falling blood pH.

los.do: Distinguish innate from adaptive immunity.
ek: Innate: barriers, phagocytes, inflammation, fast and nonspecific; adaptive: lymphocytes, specific, with memory.

los.do: Explain humoral and cell-mediated responses, MHC presentation and immunological memory.
ek: B cells → plasma cells → antibodies; CD8⁺ T cells kill MHC-I-presenting infected cells; CD4⁺ helpers see MHC II; memory cells speed the second response.

los.do: Trace each macromolecule class through digestion: enzyme, site and absorbed product.
ek: Amylase (mouth, duodenum) → sugars; pepsin, trypsin → amino acids; bile + lipase → fatty acids and monoglycerides.

los.do: Trace filtrate through the nephron and predict how ADH and aldosterone change urine.
ek: Glomerulus filters, PCT reabsorbs most solute, loop builds the medullary gradient; ADH adds aquaporins, aldosterone boosts Na⁺ reabsorption.

los.do: Sequence the ovarian and menstrual cycle hormone changes and their feedback.
ek: FSH grows follicles → estrogen peak flips to positive feedback → LH surge → ovulation → corpus luteum progesterone.

los.do: Compare spermatogenesis with oogenesis by timing and products.
ek: Spermatogenesis is continuous and makes four sperm; oogenesis pauses in prophase I and makes one egg plus polar bodies.

units.title: Developmental Biology and Microbiology
units.weight_est: DAT Biology: Genetics (developmental mechanisms) · Diversity of Life

los.do: Order fertilisation, cleavage, blastulation, gastrulation and neurulation and describe each.
ek: Acrosomal reaction and cortical reaction block polyspermy; cleavage divides without growth; gastrulation forms germ layers.

los.do: Assign tissues and organs to ectoderm, mesoderm or endoderm.
ek: Ectoderm: nervous system, epidermis; mesoderm: muscle, bone, blood, kidney; endoderm: gut and lung lining, liver.

los.do: Explain induction, determination, differentiation, homeotic genes and programmed cell death in shaping an embryo.
ek: Signals from one tissue induce another; Hox genes specify segment identity; apoptosis sculpts digits.

los.do: Describe virus structure and compare lytic, lysogenic and retroviral life cycles.
ek: Capsid around DNA or RNA, no metabolism of its own; lysogenic phage integrates as a prophage; retroviruses use reverse transcriptase.

los.do: Classify a bacterium by shape, Gram stain and O₂ requirement, and distinguish Archaea from Bacteria.
ek: Gram+ thick peptidoglycan; Gram− thin wall plus LPS outer membrane; Archaea have ether-linked lipids and no peptidoglycan.

los.do: Calculate bacterial population size after a number of generations of binary fission.
ek: N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, n = elapsed time ÷ generation time.

los.do: Distinguish fungi, protists, plants and animals by wall, nutrition and life cycle.
ek: Fungi: chitin walls, absorptive heterotrophs, haploid-dominant; Protista is a paraphyletic catch-all.

los.do: Describe alternation of generations and order plant groups by key innovation.
ek: Mosses (gametophyte-dominant) → ferns (vascular) → gymnosperms (seeds) → angiosperms (flowers, fruit, double fertilisation).

los.do: Classify an animal by symmetry, germ layers, body cavity and protostome or deuterostome development.
ek: Deuterostomes (echinoderms, chordates): blastopore becomes anus; chordates have notochord, dorsal nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, post-anal tail.
